title: Medians and quartiles

oak.lesson: Continuous variation: data handling and analysis

big_idea: The median and quartiles split an ordered set of data into halves and quarters, so scientists can compare groups in a clinical trial and measure variation without extreme values getting in the way.
goals: I can find the median, the lower and upper quartiles and the interquartile range of a simple data set.
I can use quartiles to compare the variation in two groups and to interpret the results of a medicine trial.

keywords.meaning: the middle value when the values are written in order
the total of the values divided by the number of values
the largest value minus the smallest value
a value one quarter or three quarters of the way through the ordered data
the value one quarter of the way through the ordered data (LQ)
the value three quarters of the way through the ordered data (UQ)
UQ minus LQ: the spread of the middle 50% of the data
the bell-shaped curve seen when a continuous variable is plotted for a population
variation that can take any value in a range, e.g. height
a test of a medicine on groups of people

misconceptions: The median is the middle number as written. The values must be put in order first; the median is the middle of the ordered list.
Range and interquartile range are the same thing. The range uses the two extreme values; the interquartile range uses the middle 50% and ignores extremes.
A bar chart of continuous data needs gaps between the bars. Grouped continuous data are plotted with the bars touching (as in 9A).
safety: No practical hazards. Measure hand spans gently; do not stretch the hand painfully.
equipment: Worksheets (standard and Chinese key words versions)
Board space for the class hand span data
Mini whiteboards for the quick check (optional)

slides.subtitle: How do scientists tell which patients a medicine really helps?
slides.notes: Lesson 5 of 9C, a Working Scientifically lesson. It uses the clinical trial idea from Lesson 4 and the continuous variation and normal distribution ideas from 9A. Students need rulers for the hand span data.

slides.title: Do Now: nine pulse rates
prompt: Resting pulse rates (beats per minute) of nine students: 72, 65, 80, 58, 90, 66, 75, 61, 70.
1. Write the values in order, smallest first.
2. Which value is in the middle?
slides.notes: Four minutes, in books. Ordered: 58, 61, 65, 66, 70, 72, 75, 80, 90. Middle value (the median) 70. Range 90 minus 58 = 32. Ask: why order them first? Because the middle of the unordered list (90) tells you nothing.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point out the key words box on the worksheet. The Chinese key words version has the same words with Chinese beside them.

slides.title: Wonder drug or health scare?
slides.question: 'Statins are a new wonder drug.' 'Statins in new health scare.' Two headlines about the same medicine. Trials showed statins protect most people from heart attacks, but a few may be harmed. How can scientists tell which patients a drug helps?
text: Talk to a partner: what would you need to measure, and how would you compare the patients?
slides.notes: Expected: measure something about each patient (pulse rate, cholesterol, age), split them into groups, and compare how the drug worked in each group. Splitting a large group fairly needs the median and quartiles: that is today's lesson.

slides.title: Median and quartiles
slides.text: In a clinical trial, scientists often divide the people into groups, e.g. pulse rate above or below the median. Write the values in order first.
slides.key_idea: Median = middle value. Quartiles = one quarter and three quarters of the way through. Interquartile range = UQ minus LQ.
slides.notes: Work through the 11 values. Median is the 6th of 11. The lower quartile is the middle of the lower half (3rd value), the upper quartile the middle of the upper half (9th value). With an even number of values the median is halfway between the two middle values. Interquartile range here is 7 minus 3 = 4.

slides.title: Why use the interquartile range?
text: Height shows continuous variation: a bell-shaped normal distribution.
The interquartile range is the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
It ignores extreme values, so it is better than the range for comparing two groups.
Small interquartile range: little variation. Large: a lot of variation.
slides.key_idea: The interquartile range measures variation without being biased by extreme values.
slides.notes: One very tall student makes the range huge but barely changes the interquartile range. On a normal distribution, the median is in the middle of the bell and the quartiles sit either side of it. Point out that most people are near the median and few are far from it.

slides.title: Leaves on two trees of the same species

chart.title: Number of leaves of each length

text: Tree A: narrow interquartile range. Most leaves are about the same length.
Tree B: wide interquartile range. A lot of variation.
On which tree would you find leaves much shorter or longer than the others?
slides.key_idea: A wide interquartile range means more variation in the population.
slides.notes: Both trees have the same median (about 5 cm) but Tree B has far more variation. Answer: Tree B, because its distribution is wider, so more leaves are far from the median. This is the book's diagram E in chart form.

slides.title: Statins: who does the drug help?

chart.title: Change in risk of heart attack after taking statins (%)

text: Patients were measured for how well they absorb cholesterol and split into quartiles (boundaries 107, 126, 148).
In three quartiles the risk fell. In the top quartile it rose.
Splitting the data shows the drug helps most people, but not everyone.
slides.key_idea: Quartiles let scientists compare groups inside a large set of data.
slides.notes: Interquartile range of the cholesterol absorption index: 148 minus 107 = 41. Both headlines in the Hook contain some truth: the drug lowers risk for about three quarters of patients but may raise it for the top quartile. This is why doctors test patients before prescribing.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: In the ordered set 1 2 3 3 4 5 6 7 7 8 9, what is the lower quartile?
UQ is 7 and LQ is 3. What is the interquartile range?
Does the interquartile range use the smallest and largest values? Yes or no.
What shape is a normal distribution?
slides.notes: Answers: order to 3 4 5 7 9, median 5; 3 (the 3rd value); 4; no, it uses the middle 50% only; a bell shape, symmetrical about the median.

slides.title: Class data: hand span
slides.aim: Collect the hand spans of the class and find the median, quartiles and interquartile range.
equipment: the class table on the board
method: Spread one hand flat on the desk. Measure from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger in cm, to one decimal place.
Write your value on the board.
Copy the class values on to your worksheet in order, smallest first.
Find the median, then the lower and upper quartiles.
Calculate the interquartile range. Is the class data roughly a normal distribution?
slides.safety: No hazards. Measure gently; do not stretch the hand.
slides.notes: Six minutes for the data collection, then the worksheet. With 30 values the median is halfway between the 15th and 16th; the quartiles are near the 8th and 23rd values. Accept small differences in method for the quartiles; the idea of quarters matters more than the exact rule at this stage.

slides.title: Which headline is fairer?
slides.prompt: 'Statins are a new wonder drug' and 'Statins in new health scare' both describe the same trial. Using the quartile results, which headline is fairer? Could both be true?
frames: The results show that for ___ of the patients the risk ___.
Both could be partly true because ___.
slides.notes: Expected: for three quarters of the patients the risk of a heart attack fell by 25 to 38%, so 'wonder drug' describes most patients; the top quartile's risk rose by 16.6%, so 'health scare' describes a minority. A fair report would give both. Link back to bias from 9B if the class has done it.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: Write these values in order and give the median: 12, 5, 9, 20, 7.
The upper quartile is 30 and the lower quartile is 18. Calculate the interquartile range.
What does a small interquartile range tell you about a population?
slides.notes: Answers: 5, 7, 9, 12, 20, median 9; 12; the individuals show little variation (the middle 50% of values are close together).

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Ecology: how scientists estimate how many organisms live in an area, and how they are spread out.
points: Order the values first. The median is the middle value.
Quartiles are one quarter and three quarters of the way through; interquartile range = UQ minus LQ.
The interquartile range measures the variation in the middle 50% and ignores extreme values.
Splitting trial data into quartiles shows who a medicine helps and who it does not.

challenge.q: In a statin trial, patients were measured for their ability to absorb cholesterol and split into quartiles. The table shows the change in their risk of a heart attack after taking statins.

rows: Change in risk of heart attack (%)

parts.text: Explain why the data for cholesterol absorption were split into quartiles.
The quartile boundaries of the cholesterol absorption index were 107, 126 and 148. Calculate the interquartile range.
Explain what the results show about the effect of cholesterol absorption on how well statins reduce the risk of a heart attack.

challenge.q: Explain why the interquartile range is more useful than the range for comparing the variation in two different groups.

worksheet.my_thinking: A newspaper says 'the average family has 1.7 children'. Which kind of average is this, and why can no family have 1.7 children? When would the median be more useful than the mean?
exit: Write these values in order and give the median: 12, 5, 9, 20, 7.
The upper quartile is 30 and the lower quartile is 18. Calculate the interquartile range.
What does a small interquartile range tell you about a population?

core: a) 2, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9. b) Median 6. c) Range 9 minus 2 = 7.

a) 25.1 to 25.5: 1; 25.6 to 26.0: 3; 26.1 to 26.5: 4; 26.6 to 27.0: 6; 27.1 to 27.5: 7; 27.6 to 28.0: 5; 28.1 to 28.5: 4; 28.6 to 29.0: 5; 29.1 to 29.5: 1 (total 36). b) Bars touching, x-axis foot length (cm) in groups, y-axis number of students. c) 36 values: the median lies between the 18th and 19th values, which are both in the 27.1 to 27.5 group. d) Roughly, yes: the bars rise to a peak in the middle group and fall away on both sides (a bell shape), although the 28.6 to 29.0 group is a little higher than a perfect bell.
stretch: a) 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 21, 22, 25, 28, 34, 35. b) Median = 17 (the 8th of 15 values). c) LQ = 11 (4th value), UQ = 25 (12th value). d) Interquartile range = 25 minus 11 = 14.
Class results. Check that the values were ordered first and that the median is the middle value (halfway between the two middle values for an even number).
challenge: a) To divide the patients into four equal-sized groups by their cholesterol absorption, so the effect of the drug could be compared between people who absorb little and people who absorb a lot. b) 148 minus 107 = 41. c) Secure answer: statins reduced the risk of a heart attack for patients in the lowest three quartiles (by 37.7%, 34.3% and 24.7%), and the benefit got smaller as cholesterol absorption increased. For the top quartile the risk rose by 16.6%, so the drug helped most patients but may harm those who absorb the most cholesterol.

Secure answer: the range uses only the two extreme values, so one unusually large or small value changes it a lot and can bias the comparison. The interquartile range shows the spread of the middle 50% of the data, which is not affected by extreme values, so it gives a fairer comparison of the variation in the two groups.
exit: The individuals show little variation: the middle 50% of values are close together.
answers.my_thinking: It is the mean (total children divided by number of families); children come in whole numbers, so a mean of 1.7 does not describe any real family. The median is more useful when a few extreme values would pull the mean away from a typical value, e.g. incomes or house prices.
